summary: Every review-3 finding was fixed as written: m01-q1, f05 and m10-q1 now state the fact that makes the over-cautious option pointless, m09-q4's wrong option has its re-check, M1 card 1 says a defined request is ready, and check.mjs is clean (must_fix 0, should_fix 0, no standard findings, links fine). Nothing broke: every changed number re-adds, and the card edits in M6, M9 and M10 kept their meaning. The blind clue test's pick in m01-q1 is ruled out by the founder's own message and by M1 card 1, so the key stands, and the questions have no must-fix left. The programme is not ready under the Module Standard, though. In seven of the ten modules the tasks ask learners to describe, plan or explain, not to work on data in a free tool, so practice scores 3. Those modules' minutes (90, and 120 for pandas) are then far more than the work fills. Cards that cram several ideas without a worked case hold M5, M6 and M7's explanation at 3. M1's outcome and the phone and jargon gaps in M2 and M7 need fixing too. All 19 dimensions below 4 belong to the Course Architect, and each finding gives the exact change.
strengths: The three review-3 rebuilds pass the self-test. If the founder had only said “orders feel slower”, asking her would be right (m01-q1). If the screen fault had hit only rural tablets, a re-survey would be right (f05). If the fee were untried in Tier-3 cities, a pilot would be right (m10-q1). Each why_wrong says so.

The arithmetic re-adds exactly: m10-q1 (70% of ₹60 lakh = ₹42 lakh at risk against ₹4 lakh of returns), f05 (30% of 2,000 = 600), m01-q3 (₹1.84–2.075 lakh, ₹1.0–1.25 lakh, ₹8 lakh), m10-q2 (70/80/90/420), m10-q4 (₹38 lakh × 60% ≈ ₹23 lakh − ₹15 lakh), f11 (84 against 75) and f14 (10.9%).

Feedback is consistent across all 40 quiz questions. Every explanation gives the reason, and every why_wrong names each wrong option's mistake, usually with the situation in which it would be right. The cards clue test answered all 40 from the Learn cards (40 of 40, every one marked taught), so rule 13 holds.

The setting is Indian and current throughout: ₹ and lakh, GST, PIN codes, kirana stores, Diwali and IPL, Tier-3 COD, the DPDP Act, 2023, pandas 3.0's Copy-on-Write change, XLOOKUP's exact default, and Copilot's paid capacity with a free route beside it.

The new M9 card 1 worked example (Arjun's BETWEEN query that stops at midnight on 31 March, ₹8,40,000 against ₹8,12,000) is exactly the kind of real case the standard asks for: a mistake shown, found by an independent check and fixed.

findings.problem: M5 card 3 (157 words) does four jobs, with code but no output shown: running totals, ROW_NUMBER, LAG, and filtering through a CTE. The two things the quiz tests are only implied. m05-q3 needs DESC to put the latest row first. m05-q4 needs OVER (PARTITION BY city), with no ORDER BY, to give the whole group's figure on every row, while ORDER BY makes it a running figure. The card never shows a window function's result rows.
findings.fix:
Split card 3 into two cards of 80 to 160 words.
Card 3 “Number the rows in each group”: “GROUP BY squashes rows into groups; a window function keeps every row and adds context to it. Inside OVER ( ), PARTITION BY restarts the calculation for each group, and ORDER BY decides which row comes first. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY paid_at DESC) numbers each user's payments from the newest:
user 7, 28 April, ₹300 → 1
user 7, 12 April, ₹900 → 2
user 9, 30 April, ₹150 → 1
Keep the rows numbered 1, and you have each user's latest payment. Without DESC, row 1 is the first payment instead. You can't filter on a window function in WHERE, because WHERE runs first. Number the rows in a CTE (a named subquery), then filter in the outer query:” followed by the existing WITH … WHERE rn = 1 example.
Card 4 “A group's figure beside every row”: “AVG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY city) writes each city's average on every order of that city, so you can compare an order with its own city:
Pune, ₹800 → Pune average ₹600
Pune, ₹400 → ₹600
Kochi, ₹900 → ₹900
With no PARTITION BY, OVER () gives one average for the whole table. Add ORDER BY inside OVER and it becomes a running figure: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY paid_at) is each user's running total. LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) puts last month's revenue beside this month's. The first month has no earlier row, so its LAG is NULL.”

findings.problem: M6 card 3 (157 words) does three jobs with no worked case. It covers why to randomise (and how sampling differs from assignment), fixing the measure and length to avoid peeking, and reading the result (significant, not significant, don't extend, significant isn't important). It never works through one test's numbers, yet m06-q3, f10 and f11 ask learners to judge a gap against chance.
findings.fix:
Split card 3 into two cards of 80 to 160 words.
Card 3 “A/B tests answer ‘did it work?’”: keep the first paragraph and “Before you start … early leads swing by chance.”, and add: “For example, a Jaipur tutoring app split 8,000 new users at random for two full weeks: 4,000 saw the old checkout and 4,000 the new one. 160 (4.0%) and 200 (5.0%) paid.”
Card 4 “Reading the result”: “A significance test tells you whether a gap is bigger than chance usually makes. A free online A/B test calculator says that 4.0% against 5.0%, with 4,000 users in each group, would happen by chance only about 3 times in 100: a real difference. 4.0% against 4.3% would happen by chance about half the time, so it shows nothing either way.” Then move in the existing sentences from “A result that isn't significant …” to “… not big or important.”

findings.problem: M7 card 2 (“The everyday moves”) is a list of six commands (profile, filter, combine, groupby, merge, dates) plus three caveats, and none is worked through on data. The learner never sees what a groupby or a left merge prints before t1 asks them to plan one. That is “one long card doing three jobs” without a worked example.
findings.fix:
Split card 2 into two cards of 80 to 160 words.
“Filter and total, worked through”: “Priya has five orders: Pune ₹500, Pune ₹700, Kochi ₹400, Pune ₹300 (failed), Kochi ₹600.
ok = df[df["status"] == "success"]
ok.groupby("city")["value"].sum()
prints Kochi 1000 and Pune 1200. With .count() instead, it prints Kochi 2 and Pune 2: rows, not rupees.” Follow it with the existing lines on combining conditions with & and |, each condition in its own brackets.
“Join and read dates”: the merge line with how="left", one worked line (“an order with a guest customer_id keeps its row, with NaN in city”), and the existing dayfirst and format lines. Keep df.info() and df.describe() in card 3 (“Check as you go”).

m10-q1 “test a ₹49 COD fee in two Tier-3 cities for a month”: reopened, because the text changed, and dismissed. The fee has already run for eight weeks in six Tier-3 cities picked at random, a larger test on the same customers than the option proposes, and the why_wrong says so.

f05 “The average of the 1,400 answers, with the margin of error for a sample of 1,400”: reopened, because the text changed, and dismissed. M3 card 3 says to “report the share that is missing beside the result”, and this option doesn't mention the 600. A margin of error gives precision, not who is missing.
m01-q4 survey first: the product manager's goal is test scores, and the random test measured them; a preference survey answers a different question.
m06-q2 App A: 40 reviews can't show that a 0.3-star gap is real.
m03-q1 keep the later row: the 50 pairs have different payment references, so they may be two payments.
m06-q4, m08-q1, m08-q4, m09-q1, m10-q3, m10-q4, f01, f11 and f15: unchanged since review 3, and dismissed there for the facts given.
Options run (39 of 55, m09-q4 certain): it appears to predate the round-3 fixes. m09-q4's wrong option now has the same re-check, so the key no longer wins in every situation.

lessons.rule: In a module that teaches a tool (spreadsheets, SQL, Python, dashboards, AI assistants), at least one task must have the learner do the work in a free tool, on data given in the task (6 to 12 rows inline, or a CREATE/INSERT script), and hand in the result. State the expected answer in the blueprint. “Describe”, “plan” or “explain” tasks don't count as practice for the tool.
lessons.why: In Data Analytics round 4, seven of the ten modules had only describe-or-plan tasks, so the learner never opened Sheets, a SQL playground or Colab. That held practice at 3, and it made 90 to 120 minutes promise work that wasn't there.

lessons.rule: A Learn card introduces at most two new ideas. Show a command or formula together with the result it gives on a few rows, not the code alone.
lessons.why: M5 card 3 (four window-function ideas) and M7 card 2 (six pandas commands) showed code but never its output, though the quiz asked what that output would be.
